1.e4 c6 2.Nc3 d5.name: Caro–Kann Defence
1.e4 c6 2.Nc3 d5.strategy: Challenges e4 at once, and the c6 pawn already guards d5, so Black can recapture there without loosening anything. Black keeps a solid structure with the light-squared bishop free, at the cost of a slower start in development, since the c-pawn has already moved.

1.e4 c6 2.Nc3 Nf6.strategy: Develops and attacks e4, but the knight becomes a target for the e-pawn. After 3.d4 the natural 3...d5 runs into 4.e5, gaining time, and 3.e5 Nd5 4.Nxd5 cxd5 5.d4 at once gives White a space advantage with the pawn on e5.

1.e4 c6 2.Nc3 d6.strategy: Prepares ...Nf6 and a compact, flexible set-up that keeps the centre open to several plans. It is sound but passive: White takes the full centre before Black contests it.

1.e4 c6 2.Nc3 e6.strategy: Prepares ...d5 with ...c6 already played, a set-up that supports d5 but shuts the c8 bishop in behind e6. After 3.d4 d5 4.e5 Black wants the ...c5 break against White's pawn chain, and the pawn on c6 needs a second move to get there. Solid, but 2...d5 at once keeps the bishop free.

1.e4 c6 2.Nc3 g6.strategy: Prepares ...Bg7 with ...c6 already played and leaves Black the choice between a solid pawn centre and a more elastic set-up. Sound and flexible, but it gives White more options than the direct 2...d5.

1.e4 c6 2.Nc3 e5.strategy: Strikes in the centre, but ...c6 has taken the b8 knight's natural square and e5 lacks support. After 3.Nf3 Black usually has to spend another tempo defending e5, because 3...d5 4.exd5 cxd5 5.Nxe5 loses a pawn.

1.e4 c6 2.Nc3 Qc7.strategy: Brings the queen out before any minor piece; on c7 it supports ...e5 but does nothing for ...d5. White takes the centre at once and builds on it, while Black still has all four minor pieces to develop.

1.e4 c6 2.Nc3 Qb6.strategy: Brings the queen out before any minor piece and eyes b2, which the c1 bishop guards. White gains time against the queen by attacking it with the a-pawn or the knight.

1.e4 c6 2.Nc3 Qa5.strategy: Brings the queen out before any minor piece and eyes the c3 knight, which the b- and d-pawns guard. After 3.d4 the knight is pinned, but Bd2 can break the pin at any time, and White builds the centre further while the queen has nothing to attack.

1.e4 c6 2.Nc3 Nh6.strategy: Puts the knight on the rim, from where it can reach f5 to press on d4 but does nothing against e4. Once White plays d4, the c1 bishop can take with Bxh6 gxh6, doubling Black's h-pawns, although Black gets the bishop pair in return.

1.e4 c6 2.Nc3 Na6.strategy: Puts the knight on the rim, from where it heads for c7 to support ...d5. 3.Bxa6 bxa6 doubles Black's a-pawns at once, at the cost of the bishop pair, and White can also take the centre while the knight is still on its way.

1.e4 c6 2.Nc3 a6.strategy: A waiting move that prepares ...b5 but develops nothing and does not contest e4. White takes the centre at once and develops freely, while ...d5 has still to be played.

1.e4 c6 2.Nc3 a5.strategy: Spends a tempo on the rook's pawn and does nothing against e4 or for ...d5. White takes the centre at once and develops freely.

1.e4 c6 2.Nc3 b6.strategy: Prepares ...Bb7, but the c6 pawn blocks that bishop's diagonal, so the fianchetto has little to aim at. It costs a tempo while White takes the centre.

1.e4 c6 2.Nc3 b5.strategy: Grabs queenside space but develops nothing, and the pawn, already hit by the c3 knight, ties the c6 pawn to its defence. After 3.d4 d5 4.exd5, for instance, 4...cxd5 drops the b-pawn to 5.Bxb5+ or 5.Nxb5.

1.e4 c6 2.Nc3 f6.strategy: Covers e5 but takes the natural f6 square from the g8 knight and opens the e8–h5 diagonal, so Qh5+ is possible at any moment. White develops freely and aims at the weakened a2–g8 diagonal.

1.e4 c6 2.Nc3 g5.strategy: Loosens the kingside without developing anything. After 3.d4 the c1 bishop attacks g5, so Black must spend another move holding the pawn, and after 3...h6 it comes under fire again from 4.h4.

1.e4 c6 2.Nc3 h6.strategy: Spends a tempo on a pawn move that stops a bishop which cannot yet come to g5, and does nothing for the centre. 3.d4 gives White the centre with a free hand.

1.e4 c6 2.Nc3 h5.strategy: Pushes the rook's pawn without contesting e4 and loosens g5 and g6. White takes the centre at once and develops freely.

1.e4 c6 2.Nc3 c5.strategy: Moves the c-pawn a second time and reaches the position after 1.e4 c5 2.Nc3 with White to move, so Black has lost a whole tempo. White can develop and open the centre with d4 a move ahead.

1.e4 c6 2.Nc3 f5.strategy: Gives up a pawn: after 3.exf5 nothing recaptures on f5, and 3...d5? runs into 4.Qh5+ g6 5.fxg6. After 3...Nf6 White can hold the extra pawn with 4.g4.

1.e4 c6 2.Nc3 d5 3.Nf3.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Two Knights Attack
1.e4 c6 2.Nc3 d5 3.Nf3.background: Bobby Fischer played it in his youth, but it has since declined in popularity.
1.e4 c6 2.Nc3 d5 3.Nf3.strategy: Develops a second piece and keeps the d-pawn flexible: White does not commit to a central pawn break yet and plays for quick piece activity. The price is that Black can challenge e4 or pin the knight at once, so the game stays balanced and the centre is Black's to contest.

1.e4 c6 2.Nc3 d5 3.Qf3.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Goldman Variation
1.e4 c6 2.Nc3 d5 3.Qf3.strategy: Brings the queen out at once, adding a guard to e4 and eyeing f7, but takes the natural square from the king's knight and leaves the queen open to being harassed by Black's minor pieces. Sound, yet the queen may lose time moving again against a solid Black set-up.

1.e4 c6 2.Nc3 d5 3.d3.strategy: A modest support for the e4 pawn that frees the c1-bishop but claims no more space in the centre. Solid and hard to hurt, yet it hands Black the first say over the centre, and Black can take on e4 or strike with ...d4 while White's pieces are still at home.

1.e4 c6 2.Nc3 d5 3.h3.name: Caro–Kann Defence: St. Patrick's Attack
1.e4 c6 2.Nc3 d5 3.h3.strategy: A waiting move that stops ...Bg4 but does nothing for the centre or for development. Black can take on e4 or push in the centre and develop freely; the extra pawn move on the edge costs a tempo, though it is hard to punish.

1.e4 c6 2.Nc3 d5 3.d4.strategy: Occupies the centre with a second pawn and, with the knight already on c3, reaches the main line of the Caro-Kann by a different route. The e4 pawn is guarded by the knight, the centre is set, and Black has to decide how to meet the pair of central pawns.

1.e4 c6 2.Nc3 d5 3.d3 dxe4.strategy: Takes the pawn at once, so White must recapture or play on a pawn down. Black gets the first say in the type of game, and White's slow set-up has no obvious way to claim it back with interest.

1.e4 c6 2.Nc3 d5 3.d3 Nf6.strategy: Develops the king's knight with pressure on e4 while keeping the pawn tension. The d3 pawn and the knight hold e4 for now, so there is no hurry to capture: Black gets a flexible, easy set-up and decides the type of game.

1.e4 c6 2.Nc3 d5 3.d3 e6.strategy: Supports d5 solidly and opens the f8 bishop, but locks the c8 bishop behind the e6 pawn, the piece the Caro-Kann is meant to keep free. Sound but passive, and it gives White time to complete a slow set-up unhurried.

1.e4 c6 2.Nc3 d5 3.d3 dxe4 4.Bg5.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Scorpion-Horus Gambit
1.e4 c6 2.Nc3 d5 3.d3 dxe4 4.Bg5.strategy: A gambit: White leaves e4 alone and develops the bishop outside the pawn chain with a pawn down. Nothing is under real threat, since Black's pieces easily guard e7, so Black keeps the extra pawn and the bishop is soon driven away.

1.e4 c6 2.Nc3 d5 3.d3 dxe4 4.dxe4.strategy: Recaptures with the pawn, rebuilding the e4 pawn with the knight behind it. Black can offer a queen trade on the open d-file at once, and White must be content with a quiet, level ending. A sound way to equalise, not to play for more.

1.e4 c6 2.Nc3 d5 3.d3 dxe4 4.Nxe4.strategy: Recaptures with the knight and keeps the queens on, putting a piece in the centre. But developing moves such as ...Bf5 and ...Nf6 chase the knight, so Black gets an easy, comfortable game while White's d3 set-up claims little space.

1.e4 c6 2.Nc3 d5 3.Nf3 Bg4.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Two Knights Attack, Mindeno Variation
1.e4 c6 2.Nc3 d5 3.Nf3 Bg4.strategy: Develops Black's problem bishop outside the pawn chain before it can be shut in, and pins the f3 knight against the queen. The logical reply: White has to decide what to do about the pin, and Black can trade the bishop for the knight or keep the tension.

1.e4 c6 2.Nc3 d5 3.Nf3 dxe4.strategy: Settles the tension in the centre by trading the d-pawn for White's e-pawn and heads for a classical set-up. The usual bishop route to f5 is risky here, as White's knight on f3 makes a kingside attack with Ne5 and Qh5 dangerous for Black.

1.e4 c6 2.Nc3 d5 3.Nf3 Nf6.strategy: Develops with an attack on e4 but invites e5, which drives the knight back with a gain of space and time. Black has to find a safe square for the knight and ends up cramped, which gives White a small but lasting edge.

1.e4 c6 2.Nc3 d5 3.Nf3 Bg4 4.h3.strategy: Asks the bishop to decide. Black must give up the bishop for the knight and hand White the bishop pair, or retreat and keep the pin, in which case the bishop can be harassed. Either way White gets the choice between quiet and sharp play.

1.e4 c6 2.Nc3 d5 3.Nf3 Bg4 4.Be2.strategy: Breaks the pin directly: with the bishop between the knight and the queen, ...Bxf3 is answered by Bxf3, which keeps White's two bishops. Sound and quiet, but White has claimed no more space and leaves Black free to choose the set-up.

1.e4 c6 2.Nc3 d5 3.Nf3 Bg4 4.exd5.strategy: Trades a pair of pawns and opens the position before Black has finished developing, leaving the d5 pawn as a target for the knight on c3. Black must not take on f3 first, which loses a pawn, but recapturing with the c-pawn keeps the pin. Playable and level.

1.e4 c6 2.Nc3 d5 3.Nf3 Bg4 4.h3 Bxf3.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Two Knights Attack, Mindeno Variation, Exchange Line
1.e4 c6 2.Nc3 d5 3.Nf3 Bg4 4.h3 Bxf3.strategy: Ends the pin for good by trading the bishop for the knight. Black concedes the bishop pair but keeps a solid pawn structure, so the task is to neutralise the bishops with sound development.

1.e4 c6 2.Nc3 d5 3.Nf3 Bg4 4.h3 Bh5.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Two Knights Attack, Mindeno Variation, Retreat Line
1.e4 c6 2.Nc3 d5 3.Nf3 Bg4 4.h3 Bh5.background: In Noteboom–Mindeno 1927, Black lost quickly after retreating the bishop to h5.
1.e4 c6 2.Nc3 d5 3.Nf3 Bg4 4.h3 Bh5.strategy: Keeps the bishop and the pin instead of surrendering the bishop pair, but the bishop stands on a square where a pawn push attacks it again and it risks running short of safe squares. Playable, yet Black must be accurate and trading on f3 is simpler.

1.e4 c6 2.Nc3 d5 3.Nf3 Bg4 4.h3 Bd7.strategy: Steps back off the pin and keeps both bishops, but spends a second move on the same piece and gives up its active post. White gets time to open the centre while Black is still undeveloped. Passive, though safe and solid.

1.e4 c6 2.Nc3 d5 3.Nf3 dxe4 4.Ng5.name: Caro–Kann Defence: Hector Gambit
1.e4 c6 2.Nc3 d5 3.Nf3 dxe4 4.Ng5.strategy: Attacks e4 a second time and eyes f7, hoping to win the pawn back. But the knight moves twice in the opening, and the pawn could simply have been regained with Nxe4, so the move offers little over the normal recapture.

1.e4 c6 2.Nc3 d5 3.Nf3 dxe4 4.Nxe4.strategy: Regains the pawn at once with the knight from c3, which also removes the pawn that attacks the knight on f3. Material is level, the knight stands in the centre, and White has the more active pieces in a balanced game.

1.e4 c6 2.Nc3 d5 3.Nf3 dxe4 4.Ne5.strategy: Moves the attacked knight to e5 but leaves it unsupported: ...Qd4 hits it at once, so White has to defend it or move it again while Black develops. It loses time against the simple recapture on e4.
